introduction: On this second Sunday of Lent, Abraham climbs the mountain with Isaac, ready to give God everything, and God provides. Paul draws the lesson: God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all. On another mountain, Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John, and the Father's voice tells them who he is. Let us listen to him today, so that the glory we glimpse may carry us through the cross to Easter.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God is for us, and he has given us his own Son. Let us bring him our prayers with confidence.
intentions: For the Church: that, listening to the beloved Son, she may lead all people to the light of his face. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are asked to give up what they love most: that, like Abraham, they may trust that God will provide. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the sick, the grieving and all who feel abandoned: that they may know that God is for them and that nothing is beyond his care. Let us pray to the Lord.
For catechumens preparing for Easter: that they may come to know Christ more deeply each day of this Lent. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may make time this week to listen to Jesus in prayer and in the Scriptures. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: God our Father, you did not spare your own Son. Open our ears to listen to him, and lead us from the mountain of prayer to the joy of the Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Listen to him
reflection.body:
The first reading is one of the hardest stories in the Bible. God tells Abraham: "Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love." Abraham obeys, and at the last moment God stops his hand. The angel says, "since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me." God never wanted Isaac's death. He wanted Abraham's trust, and he gave the ram himself.

The Church has long read this story in the light of Calvary. What God spared Abraham, he did not spare himself. Paul says it plainly: "He who didn't spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?" That is why Paul can ask, "If God is for us, who can be against us?"

In the Gospel, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and they see him transfigured, his clothing dazzling white, with Moses and Elijah beside him. Peter does not know what to say, so he offers to build three tents: "Rabbi, it is good for us to be here." Then a cloud covers them and the Father speaks: "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him."

The vision ends quickly. Suddenly "they saw no one with them any more, except Jesus only." They have to go back down the mountain, toward Jerusalem and the cross. But they go down having seen who he really is.

Lent is not only about giving things up. It is also about listening. This week, choose a few minutes each day to read a short passage of the Gospel slowly and ask: what is the Son saying to me today? When the road becomes hard, remember the mountain: the one who walks to the cross is the beloved Son, and he does not leave us.
